column4: God names His own straight road, commands following it, and opposes the many "ٱلسُّبُل" that scatter walkers from it.
God promises to show believers the "سُنَن" of those before them: guidance is a received, already-walked course.
Obedience places a person with those God has favoured ("أَنْعَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْهِم"), identifying the human company behind the requested road.
After naming the prophetic line, the Prophet is told, "فَبِهُدَىٰهُمُ ٱقْتَدِهْ"—walk after their guidance.
هَدَىٰنِى joins "صِرَٰطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ" to "دِينًۭا قِيَمًۭا"; guided road, uprightness, and lived religion meet in one sentence.
God takes responsibility for the direction of the path ("قَصْدُ ٱلسَّبِيل") while some routes are crooked ("جَآئِر").
Mountains, rivers, and "سُبُل" are set in the earth "لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ": a made landscape gives the traveller a way.
عَلَٰمَٰت and the star are explicit landmarks by which people "يَهْتَدُونَ".
Stars are made so people may find their way through the darknesses of land and sea ("لِتَهْتَدُوا۟").
God makes broad mountain passes, "فِجَاجًۭا سُبُلًۭا", so that people may be guided.
The One who spreads the earth makes paths in it ("سُبُلًۭا") and sends water: a traversable ground is also provided for.
The earth is made a cradle and furnished with paths "لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ", a direct parallel to the prepared road.
The earth is made "ذَلُولًۭا"—yielding underfoot—and people are told to walk its shoulders and eat its provision.
God makes the earth a spread carpet ("بِسَاطًۭا"), the ground beneath a travelled way.
The carpeted earth is for taking wide mountain roads, "سُبُلًۭا فِجَاجًۭا".
The first House is blessed and "هُدًۭى لِّلْعَٰلَمِينَ": the house named at the end of guidance is itself a guide for the worlds.
The House contains clear "ءَايَٰت", gives security to the arrival, and makes pilgrimage incumbent on whoever can find a "سَبِيلًا" to it.
Abraham is shown the site of the House and commanded to purify it for worshippers, placing worship at the destination of a shown way.
The pilgrimage call brings people on foot and on lean mounts from every deep mountain track ("فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ").
The Kaʿbah, the Sacred House, is made a "قِيَٰمًۭا لِّلنَّاس"—a standing support for people—beside the root of uprightness.
Ṣafā and Marwah are God's "شَعَآئِر"; traversing between two visible signs turns a route to the House into worship.
On the pilgrimage route, departure from ʿArafāt reaches the Sacred Landmark ("ٱلْمَشْعَرِ ٱلْحَرَام") and remembers God who guided the travellers after they had been astray.
Moses, travelling toward Madyan, asks to be guided to "سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيل"—the middle or right course of the road.
The lost person is bewildered on earth ("فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ حَيْرَانَ") while companions call him back "إِلَى ٱلْهُدَى".
وَوَجَدَكَ ضَآلًّۭا فَهَدَىٰ holds lostness and being led together in the compact reversal that closes Fātiḥah.
Pharaoh goes before his people ("يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ") and leads them into the Fire: the anti-guide reaches an opposite water-place.
Iblīs vows to sit in ambush on God's straight road, "صِرَٰطَكَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ".
The ambush spreads from before, behind, right, and left, making the straight line's surrounding exposure visible.
The covenant with Adam's children forbids worshipping Satan, the rival who turns walkers from their road.
وَأَنِ ٱعْبُدُونِى ۚ هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ explicitly identifies worship with the straight path.
Satan has led a great multitude astray ("أَضَلَّ ... جِبِلًّۭا كَثِيرًۭا") immediately after the path-command.
Jesus says worship the Lord of both speaker and hearers; "هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ".
Jesus repeats that shared lordship and worship are the straight road.
Jesus again joins "فَٱعْبُدُوهُ" to "هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ".
The command "فَٱهْدُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطِ ٱلْجَحِيمِ" keeps guidance and road but reverses their destination.
Moses is told to make for the servants a dry road in the sea ("طَرِيقًۭا فِى ٱلْبَحْرِ يَبَسًۭا").
Whoever takes Satan as patron is led astray by him and then "guided" to the punishment of the Blaze, a deliberately inverted guide.
Satan makes the people's work fair and bars them from the way ("عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيل"), leaving them unguided.
Turning from the Merciful's reminder assigns a devil as a close companion, an alternative leader.
Those companions bar people from the path ("عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيل") while the people think themselves guided.
Following desire causes a ruler to stray from God's way ("سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ"), contrasting straight judgement with an off-course will.
The arrogant refuse the way of right ("سَبِيلَ ٱلرُّشْد") yet take the way of error ("سَبِيلَ ٱلْغَىّ").
A prior people went astray, led many astray, and wandered from the level way ("سَوَآءِ ٱلسَّبِيل").
Disbelief coupled with barring others from God's way is described as straying far away.
Those who disbelieve and wrong cannot be forgiven or guided to a way.
The withheld way is specified as the road of Hell ("طَرِيقَ جَهَنَّمَ").
Whoever follows God's guidance will neither go astray ("يَضِلُّ") nor be wretched.
When guidance comes from God, those who follow it have neither fear nor grief: the traveller's instruction is to follow.
God says, "إِنَّا هَدَيْنَٰهُ ٱلسَّبِيلَ", then opens the two responses, grateful or ungrateful.
The human being is shown the two high roads ("ٱلنَّجْدَيْنِ"), making guidance a choice of track.
The Creator proportioned, measured, and guided ("قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ"); guidance is fitting each thing to its course.
Moses describes the Lord who gives every thing its creation and then guides it ("ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ").
After creating the human, God makes the way easy for him ("ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ").
Remaining straight on the way ("ٱسْتَقَٰمُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلطَّرِيقَةِ") is answered with abundant water, joining a maintained course to provision.
The address is for whoever wills among people to go straight ("يَسْتَقِيمَ").
The Prophet and those who turn with him are commanded, "فَٱسْتَقِمْ كَمَآ أُمِرْتَ"—continue straight as commanded.
The messenger calls to one God, then commands, "فَٱسْتَقِيمُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِ" and seek forgiveness.
Those who say their Lord is God and then remain straight ("ٱسْتَقَٰمُوا۟") receive the angels' reassurance.
Confessing God as Lord and then standing straight removes fear and grief, like following received guidance.
The addressee is affirmed as one of the messengers: a guide is placed before a people.
The messenger is explicitly "عَلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ".
At the dividing Day the criminals are told, "ٱمْتَٰزُوا۟ ٱلْيَوْمَ"—separate yourselves—before the worship-and-path address resumes.
Holding fast to God ("يَعْتَصِمۢ بِٱللَّه") is described as being guided to a straight road.
Those who believe and hold fast are brought into mercy and guided to God by a straight road.
By the revelation God guides seekers of His pleasure to "سُبُلَ ٱلسَّلَٰم" and then to a straight road.
God may leave one in error or set one upon a straight road, making the two outcomes stand together.
Chosen kin, descendants, and brothers are guided "إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ".
وَهَٰذَا صِرَٰطُ رَبِّكَ مُسْتَقِيمًۭا follows detailed signs: the road is legible because its signs have been set out.
God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight road.
The Lord is "عَلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ" even in the scene of creatures held by their forelocks.
The Book brings people from darkness to light, toward the road of the Mighty, the Praised.
God calls the protected return to Him "صِرَٰطٌ عَلَىَّ مُسْتَقِيمٌۭ".
Abraham is chosen and guided to a straight road, a predecessor whose course can be followed.
The Qur'an guides to what is more upright ("لِلَّتِى هِىَ أَقْوَمُ").
Abraham asks his father to follow him so he may guide him to a level road ("صِرَٰطًۭا سَوِيًّۭا").
Believers are guided to good speech and to the road of the Praised ("صِرَٰطِ ٱلْحَمِيدِ").
Faith in the revealed truth is followed by God's guidance to a straight road.
The messenger calls the hearers to a straight road.
Clear verses are sent down, and God guides whom He wills to a straight road.
Those who strive for God are guided to "سُبُلَنَا"—His plural ways—under His companionship.
Submitting one's face to God while doing good grasps the firmest handhold, the secure attachment of the traveller.
The believing man says, "ٱتَّبِعُونِ أَهْدِكُمْ سَبِيلَ ٱلرَّشَادِ": follow me and I will guide you to the path of rightness.
The revealed spirit is made a light by which the messenger guides to a straight road.
The messenger is told to hold fast to revelation because he is upon a straight road.
The Prophet is placed on a "شَرِيعَةٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلْأَمْر" and told to follow it rather than the desires of the unknowing.
The Qur'an confirms earlier revelation and guides to truth and a straight road.
Forgiveness and completion of favour culminate in God's guidance of the Prophet to a straight road.
In the contested change of direction, God guides whom He wills to a straight road; orientation is both bodily and communal.
After people become divided, God guides believers to the truth they disputed, and He guides whom He wills to a straight road.
Obedience to God and messenger would bring the people to a straight road.
The question contrasts one who cannot guide unless guided with God, who guides to truth: who deserves to be followed?
Every people has a guide ("هَادٍۢ"), placing the advancing guide in the Qur'an's account of communities.
Each acts according to his manner, while God knows who is better guided in way ("أَهْدَىٰ سَبِيلًۭا").
Whom God guides is guided, and for whom He leaves astray no directing patron can be found.
The messenger is affirmed to be upon straight guidance ("هُدًۭى مُّسْتَقِيمٍ") amid competing rites.
God guides through the darknesses of land and sea and sends winds before mercy; navigation becomes a sign of divine leading.
Even while keeping parental kindness, the believer is told to follow the way of the one who turns to God ("سَبِيلَ مَنْ أَنَابَ إِلَىَّ").
God speaks truth and guides to the way ("يَهْدِى ٱلسَّبِيلَ").
Patient, certain people from Israel are made leaders ("أَئِمَّةًۭ") who guide by God's command.
Abraham's line is made leaders who guide by God's command; worship, prayer, and almsgiving are revealed as their carried practice.
Every community receives a messenger commanding worship of God and avoidance of false powers; some are guided and some are overtaken by error.
The bee is inspired to take houses in mountains, trees, and human structures: a creature is given both dwelling and directed practice.
The bee is commanded to eat and follow the made-easy ways of its Lord ("سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًۭا"), then brings forth nourishing drink.
Exclusive worship is called "ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ", joining the daily religion to the upright course.
The Prophet says, "هَٰذِهِۦ سَبِيلِى", and calls to God with those who follow him on clear seeing.
The Prophet is commanded to follow Abraham's upright religion, making an earlier walked course a present command.
Holding together to God's rope and not dividing turns former enmity into joined hearts, the social contrary to paths that scatter.
Following other than the believers' way after guidance becomes clear leads away from their trodden communal course.
Those who split religion and become sects are disowned by the Prophet; divided religious paths oppose one road.
The communities of the prophets are one community ("أُمَّةًۭ وَٰحِدَةًۭ") under one Lord.
People cut their common affair into factions, each group rejoicing in its separate share.
Turning back to God, fearing Him, and establishing prayer provide the habitual orientation of the road.
Associators split their religion and become sects, each party pleased with its own route.
One religion is ordained to Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad; the later split is contrasted with that shared course.
The people claim to find their fathers on a "أُمَّة" and follow their tracks, an inherited path that may be unexamined.
Each town repeats the claim that it follows ancestors' tracks ("ءَاثَٰرِهِم"), contrasting following revelation with following footprints alone.
The condemned found their fathers astray, so they rush after their traces ("ءَاثَٰرِهِمْ يُهْرَعُونَ").
Their hurrying after the fathers continues the scene of inherited misdirection.
The Book opens as guidance ("هُدًۭى") for those who guard themselves, the textual companion of the road-prayer.
The guarded stand upon guidance from their Lord ("عَلَىٰ هُدًۭى"), a stable position rather than a merely known direction.
They buy error in exchange for guidance, making guidance something abandoned for a contrary course.
The same parabolic sign misleads many and guides many, showing that a sign does not guide apart from its receiver.
إِنَّ هُدَى ٱللَّهِ هُوَ ٱلْهُدَىٰ makes God's own guidance the measure against rival communal directions.
The answer to competing inherited identities is Abraham's upright religion ("مِلَّةَ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ حَنِيفًۭا").
The believers are made a middle community ("أُمَّةًۭ وَسَطًۭا") to bear witness, while the qiblah test distinguishes those who follow the messenger.
Those summoned to revelation answer that they follow what they found their fathers upon, an ancestral track without guidance.
The Qur'an is sent as guidance for people and clear discriminations, a public marker for the way.
Pilgrims are commanded to depart from where all people depart and seek forgiveness, keeping the route shared rather than privately invented.
Right direction is made distinct from error ("ٱلرُّشْدُ مِنَ ٱلْغَىِّ"), the boundary a walker must recognize.
The Prophet is told that their guidance is not incumbent on him; God guides whom He wills, clarifying the guide's limit.
The House is made a place of return and safety, giving the shown destination a place where walkers return.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations, the destination around which the later route is gathered.
Abraham asks for a submitting community and for God to show them their rites, a communal practice learned on the way to the House.
The passage insists that guidance is God's guidance, even where human groups attempt to monopolize it.
How can a people be guided after rejecting faith once its truth and the messenger's witness have reached them?
Believers are commanded to follow Abraham's upright religion, an earlier line of travel.
A community is to call to good, command what is right, and forbid wrong: a people can become a guiding body.
The best community is marked by commanding right, forbidding wrong, and faith, the practices that keep a group oriented.
People of Scripture are challenged for barring believers from God's way and seeking crookedness ("عِوَجًۭا") in it.
Those who purchase error desire that believers too lose the way ("تَضِلُّوا۟ ٱلسَّبِيلَ").
Whomever God leaves astray, no way can be found for him ("فَلَن تَجِدَ لَهُۥ سَبِيلًۭا").
Associating others with God is described as going far astray, a long departure from the course.
Disbelief in God, angels, books, messengers, and the Last Day is a far straying ("ضَلَٰلًۢا بَعِيدًۭا").
Repeated turns between faith and disbelief end with God's refusal to forgive or guide to a way.
Believers are told to seek the means of approach to God and strive in His way ("سَبِيلِهِ").
Each community receives a law and a way ("شِرْعَةًۭ وَمِنْهَاجًۭا"); distinct rites remain answerable to one God rather than mere scattering.
The Torah contains guidance and light, carried by prophets, rabbis, and scholars as a received route of judgement.
The Gospel confirms the Torah and contains guidance and light for the God-conscious.
Appeal to revelation is met by "what we found our fathers upon," even if the fathers knew nothing and were unguided.
The Prophet's grief is answered by the fact that, if God willed, He could gather all people upon guidance.
Signs are detailed so that the way of the criminals ("سَبِيلُ ٱلْمُجْرِمِينَ") may become distinct.
Abraham's family line is named as one God guided, beginning the sequence whose guidance the Prophet must follow.
A further chain of prophets is named as righteous, thickening the human company of the road.
More ancestors, descendants, and brothers are selected above the worlds, extending the guided line.
The guidance of the prophetic line would be nullified by association, marking worship's boundary.
The same line receives Book, judgement, and prophethood, the provisions by which a people can be led.
The Lord knows best who strays from His way and who are guided.
Guidance opens the breast to Islam, while misguidance constricts it as though climbing into the sky.
Those who kill children and forbid provision without knowledge have strayed and are not guided.
God's conclusive argument includes the assertion that, if He willed, He could guide everyone together.
One group is guided while error rightly falls on another that took devils as patrons and thinks itself guided.
Messengers from among the people recite signs; guarding oneself and setting matters right becomes the response to their leading.
The people of the Garden confess that they would never have been guided without God guiding them.
Wrongdoers bar people from God's way and seek crookedness in it ("عِوَجًۭا").
Among Moses' people is a community that guides by truth and judges by it.
The Children of Israel are cut up through the earth into communities, a dispersed people beside the image of one travelled way.
Whom God guides is the rightly guided; those He leaves astray are the losers.
Among those created is a community that guides by truth and establishes justice through it.
Whomever God leaves astray has no guide, and is left wandering in rebellion.
The messenger is sent with guidance and the religion of truth for its manifesting over other religions.
Some religious authorities consume wealth falsely and bar people from God's way ("عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ").
The first forerunners and those who follow them in goodness form a visibly preceding company whose route others take up.
God does not let a people go astray after guiding them until He makes clear what they should guard against.
Faith guides believers through their faith; rivers run beneath their gardens as the arrival of that course.
The Qur'anic admonition is healing, mercy, and guidance for believers, an interior provision for the way.
Whoever is guided is guided for himself, and whoever strays does so against himself.
No counsel avails if God wills to leave a people in error; He is their Lord and return.
Pharaoh is followed in this world and will precede his people into the Fire, completing the false-leader scene of 11:98.
God leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back.
One God has left astray cannot be guided by another ("فَمَن يَهْدِيهِ مِنۢ بَعْدِ ٱللَّهِ").
Every messenger speaks his people's language to make matters clear; God then leaves astray or guides whom He wills.
Moses is sent to bring his people from darkness into light and remind them of God's days.
God makes believers firm with the firm word in this life and the next, while wrongdoers are left astray.
Rivals are set up with God in order to lead people away from His way.
Abraham says idols have led many people astray, contrasting a created companion with the true guide.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are made for riding and adornment, furnishing the traveller with carried movement through the prepared earth.
Iblīs promises to make earthly things attractive and to mislead people all together.
Even the Prophet's desire for their guidance cannot overcome God's leaving a people astray; they have no helpers.
The Book is sent as clarification of everything and as guidance, mercy, and good news for those who submit.
God could make people one community, but leaves astray or guides whom He wills, holding their choices accountable.
Whoever follows guidance does so for himself; no bearer carries another's burden, and punishment follows a sent messenger.
Whoever is blind in this world is blind in the next and farther astray in path ("أَضَلُّ سَبِيلًۭا").
Whom God guides is guided, and none can serve as protective guides for those He leaves astray.
The speaker asks that the Lord guide him to what is nearer than this in right conduct ("رَشَدًۭا").
After guidance comes, people are held back by the demand for an earlier destructive pattern or visible punishment.
Turning away when reminded of God's signs makes a person unable to be guided ever.
Moses sets out until the junction of the two seas, a journey whose destination must be found.
At the junction the fish takes its way ("سَبِيلَهُ") into the sea, becoming the missed sign on the route.
After passing the junction, Moses asks for food because the journey has brought fatigue.
The attendant remembers the forgotten fish and its wondrous way into the sea, restoring the lost landmark.
ذَٰلِكَ مَا كُنَّا نَبْغِ; they retrace their footprints ("ءَاثَارِهِمَا قَصَصًۭا") to the sought sign.
They find the servant given mercy and knowledge from God, the guide whom their retracing reaches.
Moses asks, "هَلْ أَتَّبِعُكَ", to be taught what the servant has been taught of right guidance.
The prophets are those God has favoured; when His signs are recited they fall prostrate and weeping.
A later generation neglects prayer and follows desire, meeting "غَيًّۭا"—the contrary of the sustained worship-course.
God increases those who are guided in guidance, while enduring good deeds remain better in return and outcome.
Moses and Aaron carry the message that peace is for whoever follows guidance.
In Moses' absence the Sāmirī leads his people astray, another counterfeit guide inside a guided community.
The ending promises that the companions of the level road ("ٱلصِّرَٰطِ ٱلسَّوِىِّ") and the guided will become known.
Every messenger receives the same revelation: no god but God, so worship Him.
One disputes about God without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating book.
Turning proudly, he leads others away from God's way and receives disgrace.
The revealed verses are clear signs; God guides whom He wills.
Believers are told to strive for God, hold fast to Him, and live the religion of their father Abraham.
Pilgrims complete rites, fulfil vows, and circle the ancient House, extending the arrival scene of 22:26–27.
Honouring God's ritual signs ("شَعَآئِرَ ٱللَّه") makes landmarks an expression of hearts' reverence.
Noah is sent to his people with the command to worship God alone, establishing the prophetic road before later messengers.
A messenger among a later people repeats the command to worship God alone and fear Him.
Those who do not believe in the hereafter are deviating from the road ("عَنِ ٱلصِّرَٰطِ لَنَٰكِبُونَ").
God's light guides whom He wills to His light; the lamp image supplies an interior landmark for the traveller.
Obedience to the messenger is followed by "تَهْتَدُوا۟", making his delivered message the lead to follow.
For every prophet there is an enemy, yet the Lord is sufficient as guide ("هَادِيًۭا") and helper.
The idolaters say the messenger nearly led them away from their gods; the competing claims reveal a contest of guides.
Many hear and reason no better than cattle; they are farther astray in way ("أَضَلُّ سَبِيلًۭا").
The messenger asks no wage except that whoever wills take a path to his Lord ("سَبِيلًا").
Moses calls his earlier act one done while "ضَالِّين"—error in conduct rather than the literal lost traveller, widening the root's sense.
The Qur'an is guidance and good news for believers.
Who is more astray than one who follows desire without guidance from God?
The Prophet cannot guide whom he loves; God knows those open to guidance.
The fear of being snatched from the land if guidance is followed is answered by the secure sanctuary and provision God gives.
The shared God of Muslims and People of the Book gives a common direction within a disputed religious landscape.
Those who wrong follow desires without knowledge; none can guide one God leaves astray.
Set the face toward the upright religion ("ٱلدِّينِ ٱلْقَيِّمِ"), the enduring fitting of human nature.
The messenger cannot guide the blind away from their error; only those who hear the signs can be led.
Those who establish worship and give alms are upon guidance from their Lord.
The condemned say they obeyed masters and great ones who led them away from the road.
Obedience to God and messenger is called a great attainment, the practical following implied by guidance.
The two opposing parties are presented as either upon guidance or in manifest error, without allowing both courses to be true.
If the messenger goes astray it is against himself, but his guidance comes by what his Lord reveals.
God lets whom He wills go astray and guides whom He wills; ugly work can appear beautiful to its walker.
The believing man says that taking other gods would put him in manifest error ("ضَلَٰلٍۢ مُّبِينٍ").
Most of the earlier peoples went astray before the present people, extending the long history of lost tracks.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best are the ones God has guided and endowed with understanding.
A breast opened to Islam stands upon light from its Lord, an inwardly illuminated course.
God sends the best discourse; by it He guides whom He wills, while none can guide one He leaves astray.
Whomever God leaves astray has no guide, despite others' attempts to frighten the believer with rivals.
Whomever God guides cannot be misled, grounding the road's security in divine agency.
God does not guide an extravagant liar, a moral obstruction to being led.
On the day of turning away there is no protector; one God leaves astray has no guide.
Joseph earlier brought clear proofs, yet persistent doubt later hardens into misdirection.
